title: Going to the baths
hookLine: before going out, picture what happens at the public baths: splashing, shoving, theft, and keep your purpose (Enchiridion 4)
last: CLAY BREAKS; THAT'S PART OF WHAT CLAY IS.

cards: A public bathhouse, a busy afternoon. Steam, echoing tile, a hundred voices. Somebody cannonballs into the pool and soaks your towel.
Somebody shoves past you on the wet steps. Somebody shouts insults across the room. And somebody, while you're in the water, walks off with your sandals.
None of it is strange for a crowded bath; it is simply what happens there. This is the scene Epictetus chooses for section four: not a battlefield, an afternoon errand. Today: going to the baths.

teach.b: When you're about to do anything, Epictetus says, remind yourself what kind of activity it is. If you're going out to bathe, picture what happens at the baths: people who splash you, push, insult you, steal.
Nothing mysterious; just honest weather for that place. Having pictured it, say to yourself: I want to bathe, and to keep my purpose in line with nature. Notice the and.
You're going for a bath, and to stay the kind of person you mean to be while you're there.

teach.h: I WANT TO BATHE, AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.
teach.b: Then, he says, if something gets in the way of your bath, you'll have the words ready: I didn't want only to bathe, but also to keep my purpose, and I won't keep it if I'm furious about every splash.

teach.h: THE BATH FAILS, THE TRIP SUCCEEDS.
teach.b: The bath can go badly and the trip can still succeed, because half of what you came for was always yours.
Today's bathhouse might be the grocery store at six, the family dinner where a certain uncle will say a certain thing, the group chat, the morning commute.
None of it is a surprise, and yet it can still ambush you, because you walk in expecting only the errand.
A one-minute preview at the door, and an and attached to the errand, changes what counts as a good outing.
And a look back at the week: year two opened with a book for the hand, then two piles, then desire held lightly, a jug, and today the baths. Each one is small enough to carry out the door.

how: Some Stoic practitioners take a moment before an outing to picture its usual frustrations and name their aim: to do the errand and stay the person they mean to be.

o: the teacher who says: go with the errand and your purpose
a builder who designed the city's public baths

in section four the aim is only to get a good bath
the aim is to bathe and keep your purpose in line with nature.

games.q: you're at the Roman baths and someone soaks your towel on purpose. what does Epictetus have you ready to say?
o: I wanted to bathe and keep my purpose; I won't keep it furious.
splash them back twice as hard.
games.why: he says to have the words ready: I didn't want only to bathe, but also to keep my purpose in line with nature.

practice: Walk through one outing ahead of you, a store, an office, a visit, a phone call, and let the usual snags appear without bracing: the line, the delay, the comment, the noise.
Then say your sentence inside: I want to do this errand, and keep my purpose. Picture yourself in the middle of the worst moment, still steady.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus, previewing an errand: picture what usually happens, then go with two aims, the errand and your own purpose. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 4: a bath, a bathhouse.

carryVoice: Your line: and keep my purpose. The errand, and the purpose: two aims at every door. A week of year two, complete.
